unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: In this unit you will learn about your five senses — seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching — and the parts of your body you use for each one. You will learn describing words like soft, loud, sweet and cold, and begin to compare things: a tree is tall, a building is taller. Most of all you will explore the world around you, stay curious, and be thankful for all the wonderful things you can sense.
unit.learningPath:
Begin with the guided teacher launch and learn a few words through pictures and play.
Listen to the Unit story and join in with repeated language.
Complete six language, speaking, early-writing and practical activities.
If you have access to live teacher sessions, meet your teacher three times each week for two weeks for extra practice — these are optional, and every skill in this unit is also fully covered through the teacher launch, story, and speaking and writing activities above.
Finish the ten-question checkpoint, then tell an adult what you can do if one is nearby — or say it out loud to yourself.

readings.title: Amal at the Market
readings.theme: the senses, body parts, descriptions and comparison
readings.setting: Home, online lesson or Grade 1 classroom
readings.passageScript: One sunny morning, Amal went to the market with her grandma. The market was big and busy. “Come, Amal,” said Grandma. “Use your five senses today!” First, Amal used her eyes to see. She saw red tomatoes and yellow bananas. She saw green mangoes in a big basket. “I can see so many colours!” said Amal. Next, Amal used her ears to hear. She heard a man calling, “Fresh fish! Fresh fish!” She heard goats and a baby crying. “It is very loud here!” she said. Then Amal used her nose to smell. She smelled warm bread. She smelled sweet flowers. She smelled hot spices from a big pot. “Mmm! This smells so good!” said Amal. A kind man named Omar gave Amal a piece of ripe mango. She used her tongue to taste it. “It is sweet and juicy!” she said. “Thank you, Omar!” Last, Amal used her hands to touch. She touched a soft cloth. It felt soft. She touched a smooth stone. It felt hard and cold. “I like to touch things,” said Amal. “Look, Grandma!” said Amal. “This melon is big. But that melon is bigger!” Grandma smiled. “Well done, Amal. You are using all your senses.” On the way home, Amal held her grandma's hand. “I saw pretty colours. I heard loud sounds. I smelled sweet bread. I tasted juicy mango. And I touched soft cloth,” she said. “How lucky we are,” said Grandma. “We must be thankful for our wonderful senses.” “Yes,” said Amal happily. “I am thankful for my eyes, my ears, my nose, my tongue, and my hands!”

grammar.title: Eyes are for seeing
grammar.explanation: Point to your eyes and say the whole sentence. Your eyes are the sense that helps you see.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: I can see with my eyes.
grammar.commonMistake: 'My eyes' sometimes becomes 'my eye'. You have two, so say 'eyes' with a /z/ sound at the end.
grammar.memoryTip: Cover your eyes, then open them wide as you say the sentence.
grammar.practice: Say the sentence, then name three things you can see: a window, a book, a friend.

grammar.title: Ears are for hearing
grammar.explanation: Cup your ears with your hands and listen carefully. Then say the whole sentence out loud.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: I can hear with my ears.
grammar.commonMistake: 'Hear' and 'here' sound the same. Look: h-EAR has the word EAR hiding inside it.
grammar.memoryTip: The word 'hear' has 'ear' inside it. Look for it!
grammar.practice: Close your eyes, listen, then name three sounds: a bird, a door, a car.

grammar.title: Describe how something feels
grammar.explanation: Touch something safely, then describe it. Choose a feeling word like soft, rough or cold.
grammar.commonMistake: Children may name the object instead of describing it. Ask yourself 'How does it feel?' to find a describing word.
grammar.memoryTip: Feel it with your fingertips first, then choose your word.
grammar.practice: Touch three things and say: It is soft. It is rough. It is cold.

grammar.title: Compare two things
grammar.explanation: Hold one thing in each hand and compare them. Add -er to your describing word.
grammar.commonMistake: Some children say 'This is more soft than that.' Short words simply take -er: 'softer'.
grammar.memoryTip: One thing in each hand, and the -er word wins.
grammar.practice: Compare three pairs: This is softer than that. This is louder than that. This is sweeter than that.

grammar.title: Use 'these' for more than one
grammar.explanation: When you have two or more things, use 'these'. Point to both as you speak.
grammar.commonMistake: 'This is my hands' mixes one and many. Two or more take 'These are'.
grammar.memoryTip: One thing: this is. Many things: these are. Wiggle all your fingers for 'these'.
grammar.practice: Point and say three: These are my eyes. These are my ears. These are my hands.

grammar.title: Ask which sense you are using
grammar.explanation: Ask this question, then work out the answer together: eyes, ears, nose, tongue or hands.
grammar.commonMistake: Children may answer with the object instead of the sense. Ask yourself: which body part is doing the work?
grammar.memoryTip: Count the five senses on your five fingers before you answer.
grammar.practice: Ask and answer three times: Smelling bread, my nose. Tasting dates, my tongue. Hearing rain, my ears.

quizzes.question: Which body part do you use to see?
quizzes.explanation: We see with our eyes; ears are for hearing, the nose is for smelling and hands are for touching.

quizzes.question: Which body part do you use to hear?
quizzes.explanation: We hear with our ears; eyes are for seeing, the tongue is for tasting and feet are for walking.

quizzes.question: Which body part do you use to smell a flower?
quizzes.explanation: We smell with our nose; hands touch, ears hear and eyes see.

quizzes.question: Which sense do you use with your tongue?
quizzes.explanation: The tongue tastes food; seeing, hearing and smelling use the eyes, ears and nose.

quizzes.question: Which word names one of your five senses?
quizzes.explanation: Touch is a sense; jump is an action, a pencil is a thing and Monday is a day.

quizzes.question: Maya holds a piece of ice. How does it feel?
quizzes.explanation: Ice feels cold when you touch it; loud is a sound, bright is a sight and sweet is a taste.

quizzes.question: Which word tells how honey tastes?
quizzes.explanation: Honey tastes sweet; noisy is for sounds, shiny is for looks and rough is for touch.

quizzes.question: Which of these can you hear?
quizzes.options: a soft blanket | a red flower | a sweet date | a bell ringing
quizzes.explanation: A ringing bell makes a sound; the flower is for looking, the blanket for touching and the date for tasting.

quizzes.question: Which sentence about our senses is true?
quizzes.options: I can see with my eyes. | I can hear with my nose. | I can see with my ears. | I can smell with my hands.
quizzes.correctAnswer: I can see with my eyes.
quizzes.explanation: Eyes are for seeing; ears hear, the nose smells and hands touch, so the other sentences are mixed up.

quizzes.question: Which sentence compares two things?
quizzes.options: This box is heavy. | This box is heavier than that box. | The box is brown. | I can see the box.
quizzes.correctAnswer: This box is heavier than that box.
quizzes.explanation: The word than compares two things; the other sentences only describe one box.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child learns about their five senses — seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching — and the body parts we use for each one. They learn describing words (soft, loud, sweet, cold) and start to compare things (a tree is tall, a building is taller). Most of all, they explore the world around them and learn to be curious and thankful for all the wonderful things they can sense.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is a beginner, about 5–7 years old, and is just starting to read. So YOU lead this unit — a teacher in class or a parent at home.

Work in short, happy sessions of about 15–20 minutes. Lots of pointing, touching, smelling, listening, tasting and playing — very little writing.

This guide tells you what to do. The Child Activity Sheet is what your child draws and colours. The Story is one you read aloud.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with a young child
sections.body:
The grown-up holds the device and reads with the child — do not leave a 5-year-old alone with it.

Ask the tutor to say a word slowly so your child can copy the sound: “Please say the word ‘tongue’ slowly.”

Ask it to play a senses guessing game: “Which body part do we use to smell?”

Ask it to make different sounds (loud, quiet, high, low) and ask your child to describe them.

Ask it to give you one more simple activity if your child wants to keep going.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for teaching absolute beginners
sections.body:
Keep it short and playful. Stop while it is still fun.

Use real objects your child can touch, smell and taste — senses are learned by doing.

Repeat, repeat, repeat — young children learn by hearing words many times.

Praise every try. Confidence matters more than being correct at this stage.

sections.title: Songs and Rhymes
sections.body:
“Two Little Eyes” — say it together

Two little eyes to see all around. / Two little ears to hear each sound. / One little nose to smell what's sweet. / One little mouth that likes to eat.

Point to your eyes, ears, nose and mouth as you say each line. Then ask: which sense is NOT in the poem? (Touch! Wiggle your fingers.)

“The Music Man” — sing and pretend to play

I am the music man. I come from down your way. And I can play. What can you play? / I can play the piano, the piano, the piano. I can play the piano, pia-piano.

Pretend to play each instrument as you sing — piano, drum, violin. This helps your child listen for different sounds.

sections.title: How to Teach This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
Repeat this simple shape over several short sessions:

1. Warm-up (2–3 min)

Greet your child: “Hello! How are you today?”

Sing “Two Little Eyes”, pointing to each body part.

2. Learn the words (5 min)

Touch a body part and say the sense: “These are my eyes. I can see.” Ask your child to copy you.

Do the five senses one at a time. Use real things — smell an orange, feel a soft cloth, taste a sweet date.

3. Play and explore (5 min)

“Touch and Tell”: put an object in a bag. Your child feels it and says “It feels soft/hard/long.”

“Shake and Listen”: shake a box and guess what is inside by the sound.

Compare two foods: “Which is sweeter?” “Which is colder?”

4. Story time (5 min)

Read the Story file, “Sagal at the Market”, aloud. Point to the words in bold and to any pictures your child draws. Ask the simple talk-about questions.

5. Activity sheet (5 min)

Sit with your child and do one or two activities from the Child Activity Sheet. Read each instruction aloud for them.

6. Wrap-up (2 min)

Ask: “What did we sense today?” Celebrate! Say “Well done!” and one thing they did well.

sections.title: Sentence Patterns to Say Out Loud
sections.body: Speaking comes before writing. Practise these spoken patterns often:
items: “I can see with my eyes.” “I can hear with my ears.”
“I can smell with my nose.” “I can taste with my tongue.”
“I can touch with my hands.”
“It is ______.” (soft, hard, loud, sweet, cold)
“A tree is tall. A building is ______.” (taller)

sections.title: Simple Check — What to Look For
sections.body: You do not need a test. Just watch and tick when your child can do these:
items: Names the five senses: see, hear, smell, taste, touch.
Points to eyes, ears, nose, tongue and hands.
Says which body part goes with each sense.
Uses a describing word: “It is soft/loud/sweet.”
Compares two things: “This one is taller/sweeter.”
Joins in the “Two Little Eyes” poem.
